title: Sealable Femtoliter Chamber Arrays for Cell-free Biology
protocol: Dehydrate clean silicon wafers on a hot plate at approximately 250 °C for at least 1 hour.
Prepare photoresist aliquots of both SU-8 2015 and a dilution in a 2:1 ratio using SU-8 thinner as the diluent.
Spin-coat the wafer with a 2:1 diluted SU-8 2015 photoresist at 1,000 rpm for 45 seconds.
Soft bake the wafers at 95 °C for 2 minutes.
Expose the wafers using a contact aligner with the membrane channel pattern for 10 seconds.
Perform a post-exposure bake for 2 minutes at 95 °C.
Develop the wafers in SU-8 developer for 1 minute until photoresist residue is removed.
Rinse the wafer with isopropanol, moving from top to bottom.
Dry the wafer with nitrogen, moving from top to bottom.
Bake the wafers at 180 °C for 4 minutes.
Spin-coat the patterned wafers again with a 2:1 diluted SU-8 photoresist at 2,000 rpm for 45 seconds.
Soft bake patterned wafers for 2 min at 95 °C.
Align patterned wafers with reaction chamber pattern using contact aligner.
Expose patterned wafers for 10 sec.
Perform post-exposure bake for 2 min at 95 °C.
Develop wafers as described in step 1.4.3.
Dry and bake developed wafers at 180 °C for 4 min.
Spin-coat undiluted SU-8 photoresist onto clean wafers at 2,000 rpm for 45 sec.
Soft bake wafer at 95 °C for 6 min.
Expose wafers with control valve pattern using contact aligner for 10 sec.
Perform post-exposure bake at 95 °C for 6 min.
Develop wafers in SU-8 Developer for 2 min, or until residue is removed.
Rinse wafers with isopropanol from top to bottom.
Dry wafer with nitrogen.
Bake wafer at 180 °C for 4 min.
Silanize all masters with ~0.2 ml trimethylchlorosilane via vapor deposition.
Enclose the master in an airtight container at RT with silanizing agent.
Mix commercial PDMS base and curing agent in a ratio of 20:1 for membrane molds.
Mix commercial PDMS base and curing agent in a ratio of 5:1 for control valve molds.
Mix 10 g of base with 0.5 g of curing agent for the membrane mold.
Mix the base and curing agent in a 5:1 ratio for the control valve mold.
De-gas both PDMS preparations until no air bubbles are visible.
Place the control valve master in a heat-resistant container, such as a glass dish.
Pour 5:1 ratio PDMS over the control valve master.
De-gas the container containing the control valve master a second time.
Spin-coat the 20:1 ratio PDMS on the membrane master by carefully pouring the mixture onto the master to minimize air bubble formation.
Spin-coat the membrane master at 1,000 rpm for 45 seconds.
Partially cure both masters in an oven at 80 °C for 6 minutes for the membrane master and 15 minutes for the control valve master.
Cut rectangular PDMS molds from the control valve master gently.
Punch inlet holes through the molded component using a 0.75 mm hole punch.
Insert a 23 gauge blunt tip needle into the hole for cleaning, if necessary.
Clean the mold exterior using cellophane tape, if needed.
Locate the reaction chambers on the membrane master using an optical microscope.
Align the control valve mold component with the features of the reaction chamber membrane.
Place the control valve component directly on top of the membrane master.
Orient the control valve inlet to the bottom left corner of the device.
Ensure that the reaction chambers and channel of the membrane master are visible inside the rectangular control valve.
Bake the aligned mold components at 80 °C for 2 hr.
Cut the layered PDMS mold away from the membrane master gently.
Punch inlet and outlet holes for the cell extract input using a 0.75 mm hole punch.
Clean the punched holes in the same way as described previously.
Plasma treat the mold (membrane side up) at 10.5 W for 20 seconds using an inductively-coupled plasma cleaner.
Plasma treat a No. 0 glass coverslip at 10.5 W for 20 seconds using an inductively-coupled plasma cleaner.
Remove the coverslip and mold from the plasma cleaner immediately after treatment.
Layer the components, placing the membrane side of the mold towards the glass to minimize air pockets between the glass and the mold.
Hydrate a device by boiling it in deionized water for 1 hour.
Set the ambient temperature to 30 °C using an inverted microscope with an incubation chamber.
Mount the hydrated device to the microscope stage holder with cellophane tape.
Wrap the edges of the mounted device with wet tissue paper to maintain local hydration.
Use two high precision closed-loop voltage-pressure transducers to modulate nitrogen gas pressure.
Connect the first transducer by 24-gauge PTFE tubing to a water reservoir in a 4 ml glass vial with a septum lid.
Connect the reservoir to the control valve inlet using a second tube terminated by a 23 gauge blunt tip needle.
Penetrate the reservoir septum with two sharp 23 gauge needles.
Connect the second transducer by 24-gauge PTFE tubing connected to a male-to-male Luer-lok connector.
Attach this to a Luer-lok 23 gauge needle connected by tubing with another 23 gauge blunt tip needle.
Assemble the assembly individually for each device.
Use the needle to connect to the membrane reaction channel.
Flush water from the reaction channel using the needle.
Input reagents into the reaction channel through the needle.
Assemble the components for the CFPS reaction on ice, according to manufacturer’s instructions.
Place the assembled CFPS reaction into the device immediately after assembly.
Start a timer once the CFPS reaction is fully assembled and mixed.
Using tubing and needle connector from Step 3.4.2, withdraw assembled reaction into tube with 1 ml syringe.
Insert blunt tip needle into reaction chamber inlet.
Detach needle connector from syringe and attach it to male-to-male connector for reaction chamber transducer.
Apply pressure (<10 psi) to CFPS reactants to fill the channel.
Remove needle when reaction is filled.
Insert blunt tube from other transducer into control valve inlet.
Do not pressurize control valve yet.
Place mounted device on stage.
Using brightfield imaging, locate reaction chambers with 100X oil-immersion objective.
Actuate control valve by pressurizing control valve transducer to 20 psi.
Focus on bottoms of the reaction chambers.
Begin image acquisition; observe growth in fluorescence inside and around exterior of reaction chambers.
Capture images every 1-3 min until steady state fluorescence is reached.
If automatically focusing stage is not available, briefly refocus each image prior to capturing.
Expose a fluorescent standard to constant photobleaching over time to estimate the rate of photobleaching.
Record the time elapsed from reaction assembly to the first image acquisition.
Select the interior of the reaction chambers as an ROI using ImageJ’s Time Series Analyzer and ROI Manager plugins.
Choose regions of interest around the interior of each reaction chamber with “AutoROIProperties” set to an area corresponding to the chamber interior, check “Add On Click”, and select each chamber.
Highlight all ROIs in the ROI Manager.
Use the “Multi Measure” function to determine the fluorescence intensity mean of each ROI through the entire image stack.
Use data analysis software such as IGOR or MS Excel for analysis.
Determine the deterministic component of the reaction by taking an inter-experimental average across all traces.
Subtract the average from individual raw traces to obtain noise traces for each reaction chamber.
Analyze gene expression noise from these reaction chambers using the same methods used to analyze gene expression noise derived from cells.
